newsitem.title: USA: U.S. auto profits rise in 1995, but worries loom.
newsitem.headline: U.S. auto profits rise in 1995, but worries loom.

text.p: Driving mostly on cruise control for a third year in a row, the Big Three U.S. automakers earned a near-record $12.94 billion in 1996, but analysts worry that the industry's profit boom may be in its twilight.

As consumers struggle with their highest debt levels in years, U.S. car and truck sales are forecast to decline by about 200,000 vehicles in 1997, increasing the temptation for automakers to boost incentive spending.
Add the resurgence of Japanese automakers, who are using a weak yen to regain market share, and the next 12 months could prove a difficult period for Detroit to increase profits.

"The big worry in the marketplace is car sales, first and foremost," said CS First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas. "What do you do to keep car capacity utilization up and how do you fend off the Japanese?"

Ford Motor Co. Chief Financial Officer John Devine said Wednesday that Japanese automakers were already gaining ground in the U.S. passenger car market. "It's going to impact us. I can see it happening in January," he said.

Americans' shift to sport utility vehicles, minivans and other light trucks is expected to continue in 1997, leaving automakers with excess passenger car capacity -- and the need to use incentives to keep car inventories from building up.
Ford and General Motors Corp. reported higher incentive spending in 1996, while Chrysler Corp., benefiting from increased production of minivans and pickup trucks, reduced incentives in 1996.
Although the aggregate amount of earnings was impressive, results varied among the Big Three.

Chrysler's 1996 profits again were the standout of the group, increasing 74 percent to $3.53 billion. Ford's profit for the year increased 7.4 percent to $4.45 billion, while GM's results, marred by strikes, fell nearly 18 percent to $4.96 billion.
The three automakers' combined results were good enough to surpass their 1995 earnings of $12.2 billion, but fell short of their all-time record profits of $13.92 billion in 1994.

What's more, Chrysler is the only one of the Big Three earning an adequate net profit margin of 5.7 percent. GM and Ford, which have long had a goal of exceeding 5 percent, earned 3.4 percent and 3 percent, respectively.
Many analysts say that, after more than three years of strong demand and muted competition from Japanese automakers, Ford and GM profits should be much better.
Ford's earnings from financial services -- $2.79 billion -- were more than double its automotive earnings.

"The last thee years in the U.S. marketplace were like a gift," Furman Selz Inc. auto analyst Maryann Keller said. "The dollar was weak against the yen and it gave Detroit a tremendous advantage. Amid this, they come up with results that are generally so-so and you wonder what's going to happen in the future."
The 1997 outlook calls for another year of strong demand, although U.S. auto industry light vehicle sales are expected to drop to about 14.9 million units from 15.1 million in 1996.
But if sales drop off more than expected, the continuing repair work by GM and Ford managements could be endangered.

She noted that GM was a "basket case" five years ago and management has done a good job of rebuilding the company's North American automotive operations. But the efforts need to start paying dividends in 1997.

Analysts say Ford's situation is more tricky because gains it makes from stronger U.S. truck sales this year will be tempered by margin pressures on car sales and losses in Europe and South America. The automaker needs to be successful in a massive effort to cut bloated costs that have left its margins at subpar levels.
"As hard as it's going to be to cut costs, hold market share, fix Europe and South America and improve North America, Ford doesn't really have much of a choice," Colas said.
